spec.title: The valet key — read who you are and what you may do
spec.intro:
A control claims "access is authenticated and authorized." That truth does not live in a slide
deck — it lives in the bytes the protocols carry: the claims you can decode out of a JWT, the
short-lived token the OAuth dance hands you in place of a password, and the assertion fields a
SAML IdP signs and an SP must read before it trusts you. You are handed real identity artifacts
and asked to read each claim's truth directly off them, then diagnose the single field where a
real tampered twin contradicts its claim.

Every value you reveal is the real parser / state-machine over the real artifact — the same JSON a
base64url decode produces with no key, the same dance order a conformant authorization server
accepts, the same window an SP computes against "now." Nothing is invented; the decode is the
answer key. Start on the "JWT · header.payload.signature" panel.

tasks.instruction:
On the "JWT" panel, select the header segment (`jwt.header`) and decode it live. It is
base64url — it decodes with NO key. State in your decode what algorithm the token claims, and
note that you just read a JWT field without any secret: a JWT is a SIGNED claim about identity,
not an encrypted secret.

hints.nudge: You need no key to decode a JWT header — try it; the result is readable JSON.

hints.concept: §4.1 — a JWT is header.payload.signature; the header is base64url, decodable with no key

hints.reveal: Decode jwt.header — it is {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, readable with no key

tasks.explain:
The header decodes to {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} with no key — proof that a JWT is signed for
integrity, not encrypted for confidentiality. Everything in the payload is readable by anyone
holding the token; the signature only stops tampering. "It looks scrambled" is not "it is
protected" — the base64url decode you just ran is the whole demonstration.

tasks.instruction:
Select the payload's expiry claim (`jwt.payload.exp`) and read its value. This reserved claim
(RFC 7519 §4.1.4) is the deadline past which the token is no longer valid — the field an
auditor reads to decide whether an access token is live or stale.

hints.nudge: The reserved claims live in the payload; the expiry one is a NumericDate (seconds since epoch).

hints.concept: §4.2 — reserved claims: exp (expiry), iat (issued-at), iss (issuer), aud, sub

hints.reveal: Select jwt.payload.exp; it reads 1718203600 (a Unix timestamp, RFC 7519 §4.1.4)

tasks.explain:
exp=1718203600 is the token's deadline as a NumericDate. Reading exp against "now" is how a
verifier decides a token is expired — and this same token's exp is genuinely in the past, which
is exactly the broken-auth leg you diagnose later. The claim is plaintext: you read the expiry
with no key, just as anyone holding the token can.

tasks.instruction:
Select the issuer claim (`jwt.payload.iss`) and read its value. This reserved claim names the
identity provider that minted the token — the party a verifier must trust (and pin) before it
honors any claim inside.

hints.nudge: The issuer is a reserved claim in the payload, a URI naming who minted the token.

hints.concept: §4.2 — iss is the issuer; a verifier MUST check the token came from a trusted issuer

hints.reveal: Select jwt.payload.iss; it reads the issuer URI for accounts.grcbootcamp.example

tasks.explain:
iss names the authority behind every other claim. A verifier that does not pin the issuer will
honor a token minted by anyone — so iss is the claim that anchors trust. You located it the same
way you located exp: a base64url field read off the wire, no key required.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the OAuth2 / OIDC dance builder and order the message cards into the authorization-code
+ OIDC sequence, routing each between user-agent, client, authorization server, and resource
server. The dance completes only when the client trades a one-time code for a short-lived token
and the resource call rides that token — the sim runs the real RFC 6749 state machine.

hints.nudge: The user proves identity to the IdP, not the app; the app gets a code, then trades it for a token.

hints.concept: §4.3 — the valet key: authorization_request -> code -> token exchange -> resource call with Bearer

hints.reveal: Order: authorization_request, authorization_response, token_request, token_response, resource_request, resource_response

tasks.explain:
The order is the valet-key separation made literal: the long-lived credential goes to the
authorization server ONCE, and a short-lived scoped token rides every subsequent resource call.
The sim reaching its end-state is the consequence, not a stored "correct"; calling the resource
before the token exchange raises the real invalid_request, because no valet key was ever issued.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the "SAML · assertion (clean)" panel and select the AuthnContext class reference
(`saml.authn.contextclassref`). Read its value — this is HOW the IdP says the user authenticated,
the field a control like "MFA was enforced at login" actually lives in.

hints.nudge: The <AuthnStatement> says how the user authenticated; its class reference is a URI.

tasks.explain:
AuthnContextClassRef is the SP's evidence for the authentication-strength control: a ref of
PasswordProtectedTransport means password-over-TLS, not MFA. An SP that requires MFA must read
THIS field and reject anything weaker — the control truth is a string in the signed assertion,
not an assumption.

tasks.instruction:
Still on the clean assertion, select the validity deadline (`saml.conditions.notonorafter`) and
read its value. The <Conditions> window bounds how long the assertion may be trusted — an SP must
reject any assertion at or after this instant (it is exclusive, saml-core §2.5.1.2).

hints.nudge: An assertion is only good inside a time window — find the END of that window.

hints.concept: §4.4 — <Conditions NotOnOrAfter> bounds validity; the SP rejects at/after it (exclusive)

hints.reveal: Select saml.conditions.notonorafter; on the clean assertion it reads 2030-01-01T00:00:00Z (still in the future)

tasks.explain:
NotOnOrAfter=2030-01-01T00:00:00Z is in the future, so this assertion's window is open — the SP
may trust it. The staleness break (next, on the twin) turns on exactly this field: an assertion
replayed past its window is the broken-auth failure, and the verdict is the SP's computed
comparison to "now," never an authored answer.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the "JWT · alg:none twin (broken)" panel. This is a real tampered token. Select the
header's algorithm field (`jwt.header.alg`) and read it — the value here defeats signature
verification, and a verifier that honors it trusts an unsigned token.

hints.nudge: A signature only protects you if the verifier actually checks it — read what alg this twin claims.

hints.concept: §4.5 — alg:none (RFC 8725 §2.1) declares 'no signature'; honoring it accepts an unsigned token

hints.reveal: On the alg:none twin, select jwt.header.alg — it reads none, and the signature segment is empty

tasks.explain:
alg:none is the RFC 8725 §2.1 unprotected-token attack: the header declares no signature and the
signature segment is empty. A verifier that accepts alg:none trusts a token anyone could forge —
a broken authentication control (OWASP API2), mapped to IA-2 / AC-3 / CC6.1. The discriminating
field is the parser's real decode of the real tampered bytes.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the "SAML · assertion (expired twin, broken)" panel. This real twin is byte-identical
to the clean assertion except its validity window has closed. Click the single field where it
diverges from the clean leg (`saml.conditions.notonorafter`) and read its value — the assertion
is past its window, so honoring it is the broken-auth failure.

hints.nudge: Both assertions are real and nearly identical — one field puts this one outside its window.

hints.concept: §4.6 — a control is a predicate over fields; the staleness break is at <Conditions NotOnOrAfter>

hints.reveal: On the expired twin, select saml.conditions.notonorafter — it reads 2024-01-02T00:00:00Z, in the past

tasks.explain:
NotOnOrAfter=2024-01-02T00:00:00Z is years in the past, so the SP's window check (now >=
NotOnOrAfter, exclusive) fails: the assertion is stale and must be rejected (AC-3 / IA-2 /
CC6.1). The discriminating field is the parser's computed divergence over two real assertions,
not your opinion — your finding names the field, both values, the control, and the framework ref.

tasks.instruction:
In 5-7 sentences, for a non-technical colleague: explain the difference between authentication
(who you are) and authorization (what you may do), and why a JWT is a signed claim you can read
with no key rather than an encrypted secret. Then explain the valet-key idea — why handing the
app a short-lived token instead of your password is safer — and name the ONE field you would read
to decide whether a SAML assertion is still valid. Use the §3 model, not jargon.

hints.nudge: The §3 model: a passport (who you are), a building pass (what you may do), a valet key (a limited token).

hints.concept: §3 — The Mental Model + §4.4 the assertion field that bounds validity

source.xml:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!--
  OASIS SAML 2.0 example assertion (saml-core-2.0-os §2.3 / Appendix illustrative example).
  match: authored-with-citation. SCOPE-BOUNDED: the saml-xml oracle reads the fields below
  (Issuer, Subject NameID, Conditions NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter, AudienceRestriction, AuthnStatement
  AuthnInstant, AuthnContextClassRef); it does NOT validate XML-DSig. The <Conditions>
  NotOnOrAfter (2030-01-01T00:00:00Z) is the staleness break's target — compared to a supplied
  "now" by evaluateConditions(). AuthnContextClassRef is PasswordProtectedTransport per
  saml-core §2.7.2.2 + the SAML AuthnContext spec.
-->
<saml:Assertion
    xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"
    Version="2.0"
    ID="_a75adf55-01d7-40cc-929f-dbd8372ebdfc"
    IssueInstant="2024-01-01T12:00:00Z">
  <saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com/saml</saml:Issuer>
  <saml:Subject>
    <saml:NameID Format="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress">jane.auditor@example.com</saml:NameID>
    <saml:SubjectConfirmation Method="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:cm:bearer">
      <saml:SubjectConfirmationData NotOnOrAfter="2030-01-01T00:00:00Z" Recipient="https://sp.example.org/acs"/>
    </saml:SubjectConfirmation>
  </saml:Subject>
  <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2024-01-01T11:59:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2030-01-01T00:00:00Z">
    <saml:AudienceRestriction>
      <saml:Audience>https://sp.example.org/saml</saml:Audience>
    </saml:AudienceRestriction>
  </saml:Conditions>
  <saml:AuthnStatement AuthnInstant="2024-01-01T12:00:00Z" SessionIndex="_be9967abd904ddcae3c0eb4189adbe3f71e327cf93">
    <saml:AuthnContext>
      <saml:AuthnContextClassRef>urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport</saml:AuthnContextClassRef>
    </saml:AuthnContext>
  </saml:AuthnStatement>
</saml:Assertion>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!--
  Tampered twin of saml-assertion.xml for the Diff-the-Trace round: byte-identical EXCEPT the
  <Conditions> NotOnOrAfter (and the matching SubjectConfirmationData NotOnOrAfter) is set to a
  PAST instant (2024-01-02T00:00:00Z). The break is the stale window — evaluateConditions()
  computes now >= NotOnOrAfter against a supplied "now", so the staleness is the parser's
  computed verdict, never an authored answer. match: authored-with-citation
  (saml-core-2.0-os §2.5.1.2 — NotOnOrAfter is exclusive). Maps to AC-3 / IA-2 / CC6.1.
-->
<saml:Assertion
    xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"
    Version="2.0"
    ID="_a75adf55-01d7-40cc-929f-dbd8372ebdfc"
    IssueInstant="2024-01-01T12:00:00Z">
  <saml:Issuer>https://idp.example.com/saml</saml:Issuer>
  <saml:Subject>
    <saml:NameID Format="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress">jane.auditor@example.com</saml:NameID>
    <saml:SubjectConfirmation Method="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:cm:bearer">
      <saml:SubjectConfirmationData NotOnOrAfter="2024-01-02T00:00:00Z" Recipient="https://sp.example.org/acs"/>
    </saml:SubjectConfirmation>
  </saml:Subject>
  <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2024-01-01T11:59:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2024-01-02T00:00:00Z">
    <saml:AudienceRestriction>
      <saml:Audience>https://sp.example.org/saml</saml:Audience>
    </saml:AudienceRestriction>
  </saml:Conditions>
  <saml:AuthnStatement AuthnInstant="2024-01-01T12:00:00Z" SessionIndex="_be9967abd904ddcae3c0eb4189adbe3f71e327cf93">
    <saml:AuthnContext>
      <saml:AuthnContextClassRef>urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport</saml:AuthnContextClassRef>
    </saml:AuthnContext>
  </saml:AuthnStatement>
</saml:Assertion>
